ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Geriatric Psychiatry Consultation — Mark Twain — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review, seen the same day by geriatric psychiatry: the diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder, grief therapy, sleep and safety

text.paragraph: Persistent yearning, poor sleep, low mood and withdrawal a year after his wife's death in a 69-year-old writer who has also lost a son and a daughter, with passing thoughts of wishing to join her. Please assess for prolonged grief disorder and major depression, and advise on treatment, sleep and suicide risk. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the same day as his one-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Does he meet the DSM-5-TR criteria for prolonged grief disorder, and does he also have major depressive disorder?
Do you advise an antidepressant?
Which psychological treatment do you recommend, and how often?
How should we assess and manage his suicide risk, given his passive thoughts of death?
How should we treat his sleep at his age?
Is varenicline safe for him if he decides to stop smoking?

text.paragraph: Mr. Clemens, a 69-year-old writer and lecturer, is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg-Lowe one week after intake. His wife died a year and two weeks ago after a long illness. He has lost a son and his eldest daughter in earlier years and says each loss "took a piece" but that this one took the rest. He thinks of her many times every day, feels that part of himself died with her, cannot believe at times that she is gone, avoids her photographs and the places they shared, feels intensely lonely, and finds his work meaningless. He sleeps four to five hours. He has passing wishes to join her but no intent or plan and has never tried to harm himself. Away from reminders his humor and curiosity return, and he does not regard himself as worthless. He has no history of mania or of psychiatric treatment. He drinks a glass of whisky most evenings and smokes about ten cigars a day. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born on November 30, 1835, in Florida, Missouri, the sixth of seven children; at four he moved with his family to Hannibal, Missouri, on the Mississippi River. [D]

Writing for a Virginia City, Nevada, newspaper, he first used the pen name Mark Twain; he became a celebrated writer, humorist and lecturer, author of The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. [D]
He married Olivia (Livy) Langdon in 1870; they had a son and three daughters. [D]
Their first child, Langdon, died of diphtheria in 1872, at about two years old. [D]
Bad investments brought him to bankruptcy: his publishing company failed in 1894, and from July 1895 to July 1896 he made a worldwide lecture tour to earn money; he repaid his creditors. [D]
His eldest daughter, Susy, died of meningitis in August 1896, at 24, while staying at the family's former home in Hartford; the family never returned to live in Hartford. [D]

His wife, Olivia, died of heart failure at the Villa di Quarto near Florence, Italy, on the evening of June 5, 1904, after 22 months of illness; in his notebook that night he wrote that "she that was the life of my life" had died. [D]
He had his first attack of gout in Paris in about 1894 and was laid up with gout again in Vienna in October 1897. [D]
On May 18, 1905, he arrived for the summer at a rented house at Dublin, New Hampshire, in the hills below Mount Monadnock. [D]

text.paragraph: 7 later historical claims are omitted because they describe events after the index age. See the teaching note.
No medications started by this date.

tr.td: Persistent yearning for his wife, broken sleep, low mood and withdrawal from friends and work, a year after her death; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his wife's documented death a year before; resolved into the diagnosis of prolonged grief disorder at the consultation. Not a claim about his real grief.

Prolonged grief disorder (DSM-5-TR): more than 12 months after his wife's death, daily yearning and preoccupation with her, with intense emotional pain, a sense that part of himself has died, avoidance of reminders, loneliness, difficulty taking up his work and life again, and a feeling that life is meaningless; PG-13-R 41; major depression not present
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, anchored to his documented bereavements. Not a claim about his real mental health; the roster's bipolar lead is not used.
Tobacco use disorder, cigars: about fifteen cigars a day, smoking since boyhood, some smoke inhaled; first cigar within thirty minutes of waking
S — Synthetic modern coding anchored to his documented smoking since boyhood.
Chest tightness on climbing steep hills, twice in the past month, easing within five minutes of rest; none at rest; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting symptom; resolved into a diagnosis at five weeks after CT coronary angiography. Not a claim about his real heart in 1905; his documented chest pain began in 1909.

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Prolonged grief disorder (F43.81). More than twelve months after the death of someone close, he has daily yearning for and preoccupation with his wife, and at least three of the accessory symptoms (a sense that part of himself has died, disbelief, avoidance of reminders, intense emotional pain, difficulty taking up his life and work, meaninglessness and loneliness), lasting most days for at least the past month, beyond the norms of his community and culture, and impairing his work and friendships. This meets the DSM-5-TR criteria for prolonged grief disorder. The PG-13-R score of 41 agrees. [S]

Major depressive disorder. Not present. The PHQ-9 of 11 reflects symptoms shared with grief; on interview his low mood is focused on the loss, his self-worth is intact, interest and humor return away from reminders, and he has fewer than five depressive symptoms. No antidepressant is advised now: in trials, prolonged grief disorder therapy works and an antidepressant added little to it except for depressive symptoms. Reconsider if major depression develops or the PHQ-9 rises. [S]

Treatment. Prolonged grief disorder therapy (Shear), sixteen weekly sessions with a trained therapist: understanding grief, telling the story of the death, imaginal conversations with the deceased, memories, gradually revisiting avoided reminders, and rebuilding personal goals and relationships. His writing can be part of the goals work. [S]

Suicide risk. Older widowed men carry a high risk of suicide after a loss, and he has passive thoughts of death, insomnia, nightly alcohol and social withdrawal. Protective factors are strong: no intent, plan or past attempt, no firearms, his writing, his humor and the people around him. Outpatient care is appropriate with the safety plan, means safety, a telephone check and review at every visit. [S]

Sleep. Sleep should improve with grief treatment. Avoid benzodiazepines, zolpidem and sedating antihistamines, which the Beers criteria advise against at his age; use a fixed rising time, daylight and walking, and no cigar or whisky late in the evening. [S]

Varenicline. Varenicline is the most effective single medicine for stopping smoking, and large trials found no rise in serious neuropsychiatric events, including in people with psychiatric illness. It is reasonable for him; mood, sleep and any thoughts of death should be checked at each visit. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Achterberg-Lowe's intake note and safety assessment. PHQ-9 11 (item 9 scored 1). PG-13-R 41 today. AUDIT-C 3. TSH 2.2 and vitamin B12 410, normal; hemoglobin A1c 5.8 percent; sodium and creatinine normal. ECG normal. [S]

list.item: Prolonged grief disorder therapy, sixteen weekly sessions, with telephone sessions if he travels. [S]
No antidepressant now; reconsider if major depression develops. [S]
PG-13-R and PHQ-9 every four weeks. [S]
Continue the safety plan, means safety, the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline and safety review at every visit; keep whisky to one glass. [S]
Sleep plan without sedative-hypnotics. [S]
Varenicline is acceptable when he is ready, with mood checks at each visit. [S]
One planned social contact a week and a return to morning writing as early goals. [S]
Discussed with Dr. Achterberg-Lowe, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis and plan were explained to Mr. Clemens, who agreed to begin grief therapy next week. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Achterberg-Lowe continues his care; geriatric psychiatry will see him again if major depression develops, if thoughts of suicide return with any intent, or if grief therapy has not helped after sixteen sessions. [S]
